omechanical behavior in unfilled polymers undergoing strain-induced crystallization. The crystallization process significantly affects a polymer's mechanical and thermal properties, necessitating consideration in both manufacturing and application design. To comprehensively capture its effects, the proposed model employs a unique decomposition of the deformation gradient and integrates a thermodynamic framework for material modeling. This framework relies on the Coleman-Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle, which in turn requires specific assumptions about the Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential. The resulting model is capable of simulating crystalline region formation and degradation, as well as temperature changes during cyclic tensile testing. The associated boundary value problem involves momentum and energy balance equations, serving as the basis for numerical implementation within a finite element method (FEM) code. The study concludes with numerical examples illustrating microstructure evolution and temperature distribution in various material samples.

The superconducting order parameter from the $E_u$ representation interacted non-trivially with the transverse Zeeman field, causing a paramagnetic response to magnetization. This is particularly evident in robotics, where a teacher must simultaneously control multiple degrees of freedom to provide kinesthetic demonstrations on a robotic manipulator. The difficulty in providing optimal demonstrations severely restricts the scope of problems where a teacher can offer quality feedback. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed using alternative feedback types, such as the teacher's preferences or rewards, as an alternative to state-action demonstrations. While prior work has focused on developing algorithms that can learn from specific types of noisy feedback, it is clear that different tasks and teachers may require different forms of feedback. To overcome this challenge, we suggest that learning from a variety of feedback is necessary to accommodate diverse scenarios. To achieve this, we make the observation that a teacher's cost function is implicit and can be modeled as a sequence of loss functions. By applying an online learning algorithm to minimize the sum of these losses, we can effectively learn from a range of feedback, even when it is weakly correlated with the teacher's true cost function. Our proposed approach unifies prior work into a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm and demonstrates that it can achieve the same regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback used. We evaluate our approach by using it to learn a household navigation task on a robotic platform and show that it can learn quickly from a variety of noisy feedback.

By leveraging the Lagrange multipliers method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization problem can be translated into a system of linear equations, potentially benefiting from the accelerated processing provided by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain components of HHL are not compatible with Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid formulation of HHL that enables the end-to-end execution of small-scale portfolio-optimization problems on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variant with new quantum-hardware features, including mid-circuit measurement, qubit reset and reuse, and Quantum Conditional Logic (QCL). Notably, NISQ-HHL incorporates a QCL-enhanced version of Phase Estimation executed on real hardware, the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1. Furthermore, NISQ-HHL features a novel approach for determining the optimal evolution time for Hamiltonian simulation. Although this research focuses on portfolio optimization, the proposed techniques to improve HHL's scalability are broadly applicable to any problem that can be solved via HHL in the NISQ era.

This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) that allows for joint learning of ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning approach. Recent mass and orbital estimates for GJ 229B have yielded conflicting results, necessitating further investigation. Given its proximity to the boundary between planetary and stellar formation regimes, GJ 229B's atmosphere may hold the key to understanding the formation processes of intermediate-mass objects. To address these questions, we applied the APOLLO code to published spectra of GJ 229B across a broad wavelength range, yielding a refined mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$ and an effective temperature estimate of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K, consistent with evolutionary models for brown dwarfs. These results suggest an age of $>$1.0 Gyr for the system. We also retrieved molecular abundances, including a high CO abundance, and discussed their implications for GJ 229B's formation and evolution. This study provides valuable insights for the analysis of other brown dwarfs and directly-imaged planets, including those observable with JWST and future telescopes.

Focusing on the deep-inelastic scattering regime, we establish the corresponding moment sum rules for the structural functions. These moments are determined by the thermal expectation value of twist-two operators, which can be computed using first-principles lattice QCD calculations or incorporated into a model of the jet medium. We demonstrate how lattice QCD calculations can determine the minimum photon virtuality required for the Bjorken scaling of structural functions to become applicable. Furthermore, we provide the parton-model interpretation of the structural functions in the Bjorken limit and verify its consistency. In this context, the kinematic variable $x$ represents the longitudinal momentum carried by the partons, and its range extends from zero to infinity. By parameterizing the parton momentum as $x T u$, where $u$ is the fluid four-velocity and $T$ its temperature in the rest frame, the parton distribution function for a plasma of non-interacting quarks is found to be proportional to $x \log(1+e^{-x/2T})$.

unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks on specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods.

The analysis involves a model comprising an encoder, decoder, and adversary, with the latter having access to the message, a non-causal noisy transmission observation, and unlimited transmission capabilities. The decoder, on the other hand, observes a noisy sum of the encoder and adversary's outputs. A method to adapt existing channel codes for authentication purposes is proposed, and it is demonstrated that this modification incurs an infinitesimally small rate cost while enabling authentication as long as the adversary's observation is not noiseless. Crucially, this modification is not dependent on the statistical characterization of the adversary's channel, and no secret key is required, thereby facilitating a robust practical implementation. Building on these findings, the study calculates the channel-authenticated capacity and shows that it is equivalent to the non-adversarial channel capacity. The proposed modular scheme, designed for use in the specified channel model, can be applied to a broad range of settings.

The presence of lattice relaxation in the sample causes the flat band to blend with remote valence bands, leading to significant differences in the contribution of interband transitions to the plasmon dispersion and energy. Under conditions where only intraband transitions within the doped flat band are considered, low-damped and quasi-flat plasmons arise. Conversely, a $\sqrt q$ plasmon dispersion is observed when interband transitions between the flat band and remote bands are also taken into account. The plasmon energies can be adjusted through twist angles and doping levels. However, in rigid samples without lattice relaxation, both lower-energy quasi-flat plasmons and higher-energy interband plasmons can coexist. For highly doped rigid samples, enhanced interband transitions can suppress the quasi-flat plasmons. Our study highlights the importance of two key factors, the isolated flat band and a suitable hole-doping level, for observing the low-damped and quasi-flat plasmon mode in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides. The findings of this research may provide valuable insights for studying plasmon-mediated superconductivity in these materials in the future.

an expansive outflow of material, often funneled by magnetic fields into surrounding magnetospheres. The powerful winds of massive stars are generated by the scattering of radiative energy, whereas in smaller stars like the Sun, weaker mass loss occurs due to the thermal expansion of heated coronas. In exoplanets orbiting these low-mass stars, radiative heating and wind interaction can cause atmospheric expansion or erosion. Stellar magnetospheres form internally due to wind trapping, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by external stellar wind impacts. However, in both cases, stress can trigger magnetic reconnection, producing observable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to provide an overview of the underlying physics of these processes, highlighting their similarities and differences in stars and planets.

Controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling could lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductors and semimetals. In our research, we investigated magnetoelectrical transport properties, such as magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers to detect signs of the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and determine its origin. Analysis of the Anomalous Hall Resistivity suggests that the Bismuth layers alter the Hall effect scattering mechanism to an extrinsic skew-scattering type, implying that the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect is linked to elastic scattering of Cobalt free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface.

To investigate this, we chose the task of agreement prediction in Basque as a case study for a task that necessitates implicit comprehension of sentence structure and the acquisition of a complex yet consistent morphological system. Our analysis of experimental results from two syntactic prediction tasks - verb number prediction and suffix recovery - reveals that sequential models perform poorly on agreement prediction in Basque, contradicting expectations based on previous agreement prediction work in English. Lowering PET tracer doses or scanning times reduces photon counts, compromising image quality. Recent advancements in deep learning allow for the transformation of low-quality PET images, acquired with significantly reduced doses and paired with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), into high-quality PET images. However, existing deep learning methods are primarily evaluated on test data with characteristics similar to their training data, neglecting performance assessments on new acquisitions outside their distribution. We introduce a novel deep learning framework that incorporates the physics underlying PET imaging systems and models the uncertainty in its predictions by accounting for the variability in the residuals between predicted and reference images. This uncertainty-aware framework, suDNN, uses multimodal inputs, including low-dose PET images and multi-contrast MRI data, to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thereby enhancing suDNN's robustness to out-of-distribution data. Results from in vivo PET-MRI studies and various forms of out-of-distribution data demonstrate the superiority of suDNN over current methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments.

searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through the SETI initiative, with a key focus on identifying Dyson Spheres - hypothetical structures surrounding stars that harness their energy for advanced civilizations. This study examines the feasibility of constructing a Dyson Sphere around a black hole, exploring six potential energy sources, including the cosmic microwave background, Hawking radiation, and relativistic jets. Our analysis indicates that collecting energy from an accretion disk, which can reach luminosities of $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$, could be sufficient to support a Type II civilization. Furthermore, incorporating other forms of energy from relativistic jets could increase the total energy collection by approximately fivefold. Considering the detectability of a Dyson Sphere, our results suggest that such a structure surrounding a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way could be observable in the ultraviolet, optical, near-infrared, and mid-infrared spectrums via waste heat radiation, potentially identifiable using current telescopes and techniques such as spectral energy distribution fitting and radial velocity measurements.

A method to achieve this involves using active measurement tools that inject artificial traffic and assess network performance through probes. However, these tools consume a lot of resources and can only cover a small portion of what could be measured, which can lead to missing SLA breaches. The definition of this limited scope is currently handled by human administrators, who lack the scalability and adaptability needed for dynamic networks. This article explores the potential benefits of using peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the detection of SLA breaches. Firstly, we outline the principles of steering active measurement tools using P2P technology, which is characterized by a high degree of decentralized decision-making across a network through a self-organizing overlay. Secondly, we present measurement session activation strategies based on these principles, which do not require human intervention, are adaptable to network condition changes, and independent of the underlying active measurement technology.

, cutting-edge long-baseline neutrino experiments heavily rely on accurate models of neutrino interactions with atomic nuclei. These models contribute significantly to the overall systematic uncertainty due to the limited ability of existing detectors to detect final state neutrons. Next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments will incorporate three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers in their near detectors, which boast superior timing resolution and fine granularity. This technology enables the measurement of neutron kinetic energy in neutrino interactions on a per-event basis, thus providing valuable data to refine neutrino interaction models and improve neutrino energy reconstruction. Prototypes of these detectors have been tested at the neutron beamline at Los Alamos National Laboratory, exposing them to neutron energies between 0 and 800 MeV in 2019 and 2020. To validate their neutron detection capabilities, the total neutron-scintillator cross section was measured and compared to external data, yielding a value of 0.36 $\pm$ 0.05 barn between 98 and 688 MeV.

how temperature influences the attraction between tiny, chondritic particles. We observed that their surface energy decreased by approximately five times as the temperature increased. Now, we're examining the effect of surface moisture on these particles. Typically, in a laboratory setting, multiple water layers form around the particles, but in the low-pressure environment of protoplanetary discs and at moderate temperatures, a single water layer usually covers the grains. As the grains move towards the center of the disc, even this layer eventually evaporates in the warmer regions. To account for this, we tested the tensile strength of the same chondritic material using two new preparation methods: drying the dust in air and heating it in a vacuum. Our results show that for all temperatures up to 1000 K, the dried samples exhibit a tenfold increase in attraction compared to the wet samples. The super-dry samples behave similarly until 900 K, after which their attraction exponentially increases by another factor of approximately 100 at around 1200 K. This increase in attraction from wet to dry aligns with a known trend in amorphous silicates and multimineral mixtures. Furthermore, our findings suggest that aggregate growth is significantly enhanced in a small, high-temperature region around 1200 K, which may be a crucial factor in the planetesimal formation process.

Unlike unconstrained methods that disregard environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows for adapting human skills to unstructured environments, thus expanding its application scope. Despite existing studies on various constraints such as joint limits and obstacle avoidance, nonlinear hard constraints remain under-addressed. To address this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP), a framework that tackles key challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn probabilistic features from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to desired positions and velocities, avoid obstacles, and satisfy both linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also explores connections between EKMP and state-of-the-art motion planning techniques, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm.

Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we investigated the superconducting properties of a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with Rashba spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman magnetic field. Our findings indicate that Rashba spin-orbit coupling has a positive impact on s-wave superconductivity. When superconductivity is suppressed by the Zeeman field due to Pauli pair-breaking, the Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field by mixing the spins, thus restoring superconductivity at finite temperatures. This favorable effect of the spin-orbit coupling arises from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the amplitude for the propagation of a pair of electrons in time-reversed states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for sufficiently large Rashba coupling and Zeeman field, the superconducting state is expected to exhibit a topologically non-trivial nature by examining the Fermi surface of the interacting model.

However, the parabolic brush model falls short in describing polymers attached to concave or curved surfaces such as spherical particles or interfaces of block copolymers. It has been demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a boundary layer devoid of free chain ends, requiring modifications to the theoretical analysis. Although the "end exclusion zone" has been successfully incorporated into models of brushes on the outer surfaces of cylinders and spheres, the behavior of brushes on surfaces with arbitrary curvature remains unexplored. This study presents a formulation of the strong-stretching theory for molten brushes on surfaces with arbitrary curvature, identifying four distinct regimes where brushes are predicted to exhibit end exclusion zones, including regimes with positive mean curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we report the predicted scaling of the end exclusion zone size, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching with mean and Gaussian surface curvatures. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of how brush geometry influences end exclusion zones and exact strong-stretching free energies, which can be applied to model the full range of brush geometries encountered in block copolymer assembly.

To achieve this, we consider a basic model where multiple agents are instructed to act in a predetermined order, known as the action sequence. Each agent aims to maximize her value based on the actions taken by the preceding agents in the sequence. Our primary objective is to identify action sequences that yield near-optimal overall value for the agents, often referred to as social welfare. We assume that we have query access to the value that each agent receives when she acts after a specific set of agents. We establish strict limits on the social welfare that can be achieved using a polynomial number of queries, even though these bounds indicate a marginally sublinear approximation of optimal social welfare in general. However, when valuations are based on specific combinatorial domains, we can obtain excellent approximations using simple and efficient algorithms. For instance, when valuations are defined using bipartite matchings, arborescences in directed graphs, and satisfiability of Boolean expressions, we can achieve 2-approximations. We also discuss the implications of truthfulness and demonstrate how some of our algorithms can be implemented truthfully using VCG-like payment schemes. Lastly, we introduce the concept of the price of serial dictatorship, a measure that provides an optimistic assessment of the quality of combinatorial optimization solutions generated by action sequences.

a large intraplate rift zone during the Jurassic-Cretaceous breakup of the African and South American plates. By analyzing the deformation of the Central and West African rift zone, we can infer the pre-breakup history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins. Our research suggests that the development of marginal structures, such as the Pre-salt sag basin and the S\~ao Paulo High, was influenced by changes in extension direction and velocity during the continental extension process. Initially, the South American and African plates were extending east-west at a slow rate until Upper Hauterivian times, when rift activity increased significantly in the equatorial Atlantic domain. During this initial stage, the Pre-salt basin width on the conjugate margins was formed. A subsequent stage, lasting from 126.57 Ma to the Base Aptian, was characterized by strain localization, rapid lithospheric weakening, and a shift in extension direction to northeast-southwest. The final breakup between South America and Africa occurred in the conjugate Santos-Benguela margin segment around 113 Ma and in the Equatorial Atlantic domain between the Ghanaian Ridge and the Piau\'i-Cear\'a margin at 103 Ma. We propose that the complex rift history played a primary role in shaping the conjugate passive margins and can explain the major tectonic features along the South Atlantic and potentially other passive margins.

graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure provides visual evidence supporting the principle of remote epitaxy.

GeV radiation remains a mystery, and researchers suggest that hadronic emission from magnetic arrest disks around black holes could be the solution. According to this theory, particles in the disk are accelerated through magnetic reconnection and turbulence. By applying this model to the 15 brightest radio galaxies, we found that it can explain GeV radiation if the rate at which material falls towards the black hole is very low. However, at higher rates, the gamma-rays are absorbed by interactions with low-energy photons. If we consider another theory for how electrons are heated by magnetic reconnection, the model fails to match the data for most galaxies, highlighting the importance of electron heating rates. Additionally, applying the model to the Galactic center revealed that gamma-rays there are not produced by the disk around Sgr A*. We estimated the cosmic ray intensity from Sgr A* but found it too low to account for the high-energy cosmic rays detected on Earth.

By establishing essential mathematical equations and developing efficient algorithms, drawing on geometric and spline techniques, we can calculate the probability density function, cumulative distribution function, and k-th moment of the probability function. Our tools efficiently handle large portfolios and compute high-order moments quickly, making them suitable for real-world applications. We focus on long-only investment strategies, where portfolio weights are non-negative and sum to 1, and our approach can be easily adapted to other scenarios. We use a geometric representation of the stock market, where the investment set forms a simplex polytope, and the cumulative distribution function represents a portfolio score indicating the percentage of portfolios yielding a return below a specified value. We derive closed-form formulas for the first four moments of the cross-sectional returns distribution and develop an algorithm to compute higher moments. We demonstrate that the first four moments directly relate to the moments of asset returns. Our algorithms and solutions are universally applicable and include the special case of equal asset returns, which was previously excluded in some studies. We also apply our portfolio score in the k-means clustering algorithm and show that it can produce diverse and less concentrated portfolios than the standard k-means method.

Due to the rarity of stable de Sitter vacua in string theory, dark energy is typically modeled as a quintessence field in slow roll. As this field evolves, a multitude of heavy states will typically become accessible, leading to a catastrophic phase transition in the universe's low-energy dynamics after only a few hundred Hubble times. Consequently, dark energy's dominance cannot persist indefinitely, and there's at least a possibility that we find ourselves in the universe's first Hubble epoch. To illustrate this breakdown in cosmological dynamics, we employ a simplified model of quintessence interacting with a tower of heavy states, demonstrating how the universe's behavior changes as the tower becomes accessible, eventually overwhelming the quintessence field. Additionally, we explore implications for early universe inflation.

research focuses on the process of producing leptoquark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider in a manner that could provide more accurate constraints on leptoquark properties and aid in identifying them correctly. Focusing on a suitable dark-state scenario, we found that the interplay between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation can create stable atom-molecule pairs from three initial spin-zero atoms. By implementing a layer-sharing architecture, our system can process deinterlacing tasks in real-time using a single GPU. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing approaches in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

Nevertheless, conventional numerical solutions of the SWEs are computationally intensive and require precise riverbed profile measurements. We present a two-step approach to address this issue. Firstly, we utilize the principal component geostatistical approach to estimate the probability distribution of the riverbed profile from flow velocity measurements. Research has shown that the $2k$th moment of the semi-circular distribution is equivalent to the count of non-intersecting pair-partitions of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 2k\}$. This finding has been extended in various ways, and this paper aims to provide a unified extension that also yields novel insights. Assuming the entries of an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix $W_n$ are independently distributed, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, the limiting spectral distribution exists with probability or certainty. The moments of the limit can be characterized through a set of more general partitions, giving rise to intriguing enumerative combinatorial problems. Our results encompass several existing findings on the standard Wigner matrix and other related models, including sparse Erdos-Renyi graphs, heavy-tailed Wigner matrices, and banded Wigner matrices. Moreover, our main results yield new findings on these models and their extensions.

This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem.

To investigate the role of bulges in shaping the main sequence, we compared the NUV$-r$ color between the central and outer regions of 6401 local star-forming galaxies. This comparison revealed that the NUV$-r$ color, a reliable indicator of specific star formation rate, shows minimal difference between the central and outer regions for galaxies with masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. However, above this mass threshold, the central NUV$-r$ color becomes significantly redder, indicating that the central bulge is more evolved in more massive galaxies. Our analysis further suggests that star formation in bulges is more dependent on the S\'ersic index $n$ than on the bulge-to-total mass ratio B/T. Notably, the fraction of galaxies with $n$>2.0 increases rapidly with mass at $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, consistent with the turning over of the main sequence at the same mass transition. Therefore, we conclude that the growing prevalence of low-sSFR dense bulges in high-mass galaxies, rather than an increase in B/T, is responsible for the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at high masses.

However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to unforeseen program behaviors that developers did not intend. We introduce a new formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and incorporates fences that interact with the coherence layer. Using this framework, we develop an algorithm to assess reachability and determine whether a program meets specific safety requirements with the existing set of fences. Additionally, we outline a method for inserting the optimal set of fences that ensures program correctness under these protocols. This method relies on a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, which can handle various fences with different costs, making optimization more complex due to the need to minimize the total cost of inserted fences. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we have implemented a prototype and tested it on a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. Furthermore, we have evaluated the performance of the resulting fenced programs through simulation.

highly star-forming galaxies within a specific galaxy group at a distance of 2.91 billion light-years. Each of these massive galaxies contains a compact, star-bursting core surrounded by an extended disk. What's surprising is that these disks are both inactive and severely uneven in terms of their mass distribution. This suggests that a process known as "outside-in" quenching is occurring, where star formation is being suppressed from the outer regions towards the center. We propose that the uneven mass distribution in the disks is the result of gas and clump accretion, which funnels clumps towards the galaxy center, creating the compact starbursts. The location of these accretion streams is marked by a lopsided distribution of stars and gas, with additional features such as stellar warps and an irregular disk shape. The interaction with these accreted clumps, which can be thought of as minor mergers, is causing the galaxy's center to be suppressed, resulting in outside-in quenching. This process is keeping the galaxy's outer regions active and fuelled, while suppressing star formation in the center. This is the first observational evidence for outside-in quenching, and it provides a mechanism for explaining the observed relationship between galaxy mergers and the quenching of star formation.

This research introduces a novel approach to resolving this dilemma by re-examining the foregone conclusion doctrine, a concept established in Fisher v US. Our ultimate goal is to develop a framework that enables courts to determine whether any action implies knowledge already possessed by the government. In this paper, we focus on a narrower objective: creating a framework that identifies actions where all implicit testimony can be considered a foregone conclusion. Our approach involves shifting the burden of proof to the government to demonstrate that it is not relying on the respondent's truthful testimony. Building on original legal analysis and employing precise computer science formalisms, we introduce the concept of demonstrability as a central idea for describing compelled actions. We also develop a language to assess whether a compelled action forces the respondent to perform in a manner that achieves the government's desired outcome. We then apply our definitions to analyze the compellability of various cryptographic primitives, including decryption, multifactor authentication, commitment schemes, and hash functions. Notably, our framework yields a surprising conclusion regarding compelled decryption in scenarios where the encryption scheme is deniable: the government can compel decryption, but the respondent remains free to choose any password.

Typically, stars with moderate mass exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, which should give way to a faster core and slower outer layers as they evolve into giants. However, observations of KIC 9267654 suggest a rotation rate at its surface that surpasses that of its bulk envelope, contradicting conventional theories of angular momentum conservation. To address this anomaly, we refine the methods for determining surface rotation rates, confirm that the star's pulsation patterns align with previously established core and envelope rotation rates, and rule out the presence of significant chemical anomalies. Additionally, we find no evidence of a companion star that might be influencing the star's rotation through tidal interactions. Lastly, we propose possible explanations for this unusual rotation profile, including the possibility of a giant planet being engulfed by the star or the impact of tidal inertial waves triggered by a nearby substellar companion, and advocate for further research into this phenomenon.

Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) is used to treat mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) by ablating intracranial structures. To assess the effectiveness of this treatment, it is essential to segment and quantify the lesions before and after LITT using automated methods. Although deep learning techniques like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) excel in region of interest (ROI) segmentation, they require extensive annotated data for training. However, gathering such data for emerging treatments like LITT is impractical. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis (PAVAE) that generates synthetic data to expand the training dataset. PAVAE consists of two interconnected networks: one synthesizes masks and the other uses these masks to synthesize realistic lesions. To leverage existing expert knowledge, we incorporated a contrast and edge-aware technique and a condition embedding block into our network. Finally, we trained a segmentation network using both real and synthetic data to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach produces realistic synthetic data and outperforms traditional data augmentation techniques in downstream segmentation tasks.

Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal brain circuit dynamics. Despite the existence of various contributing factors, the disease's underlying mechanisms and molecular causes remain poorly understood, and no cure has been found. To address this knowledge gap, researchers have created computational models inspired by neurobiological aspects observed in animal models. Our model utilized a data-driven approach with biologically constrained parameters optimized through differential evolution, resulting in models that accurately replicated single-neuron firing rates and local field potential signatures from healthy and Parkinson's disease-affected marmoset brain data. Notably, this is the first Parkinson's disease model based on simultaneous electrophysiological recordings from seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest that our model can facilitate the investigation of Parkinson's disease mechanisms and support the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it can be applied to other computational neuroscience problems where biological data can be used to inform multi-scale brain circuit models.

This study investigates whether suboptimal offline datasets can be utilized to enhance imitation learning. The research presents a framework that utilizes offline datasets to develop a factored transition model, allowing for the extraction of a latent action space. To address this issue, we introduce Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), a novel framework that enables agents to learn from each other's past experiences without external supervision. QCD axion sector to the Standard Model can address several fundamental issues in particle physics, including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. This extension also resolves the strong CP problem and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum, allowing for critical Higgs inflation that satisfies current observational constraints. In this framework, which we refer to as the $a\nu$MSM, we investigate the properties of dark matter, finding that it cannot be explained by primordial black holes due to the model's unique characteristics. As a result, we are left with a multicomponent dark matter system consisting of axions and sterile neutrinos, which enables us to relate the axion parameters to the neutrino parameters. Our analysis includes various mechanisms for dark matter production, including axion production through misalignment and topological defect decay, as well as sterile neutrino production through resonant and non-resonant processes and in a CPT-symmetric universe.

To better understand these complex networks, scientists are employing advanced mathematical techniques and deep graph theory to quantify their hidden geometric patterns and study dynamic processes that occur within them. This study utilizes a recently developed model for the self-organization of triangles to create networks of interconnected triangles and investigates how field-driven spin reversal processes unfold within these structures. By introducing antiferromagnetic interactions between the Ising spins attached to the nodes, the model effectively creates a state of geometric frustration, a phenomenon recognized in condensed matter physics as the origin of novel effects. The dynamic model allows for a gradual shift from pairwise to triangle-based interactions, controlled by a parameter, resulting in a transition from spin frustration to mesoscopic ordering influenced by the complex arrangement of triangles. We demonstrate how the balance between these interactions affects the shape of the hysteresis loop and how the fluctuations in the accompanying Barkhausen noise exhibit robust indicators of self-organized criticality, a phenomenon induced solely by the network geometry and not by magnetic disorder.

We've developed a framework using soft-collinear effective theory to account for the impact of massive quarks in differential distributions, covering both primary contributions from heavy-quark initiated hard scatterings and secondary effects from gluons splitting into heavy-quark pairs. Specifically, we're examining the Drell-Yan process and its relation to vector-boson transverse momentum and beam thrust. The theoretical framework depends on the relative scales of hard, mass, and transverse momentum, ranging from a decoupling limit where transverse momentum is much smaller than mass to a massless limit where mass is much smaller than transverse momentum. The conventional method for describing optical properties is the velocity gauge, characterized by a linear connection to the vector potential. However, a transformation allowing the use of the electric field in finite systems is possible, resulting in the dipole gauge, which is an extension of Peierls substitution to multiple orbitals. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods, with a focus on gauge invariance, in tight-binding models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions. We focus on two-dimensional materials and develop first-principle models to calculate the response to electromagnetic fields in both linear and strong excitations. By comparing the results to fully converged first-principle calculations, we determine the accuracy of the tight-binding models. Our findings show that the dipole gauge provides a more accurate description than the velocity gauge in all cases, with the main issue in the velocity gauge being the imperfect cancellation of paramagnetic and diamagnetic currents. We formulate a sum rule to enforce this cancellation, which corrects the tight-binding models in the velocity gauge and yields excellent agreement with the dipole gauge, thus ensuring gauge invariance.

Our findings reveal that when these networks rely on a single type of tensor for erasure correction, they exhibit paradoxical behavior where they either remain unchanged or undergo a significant transformation in response to an increase in energy. This phenomenon arises from the networks' ability to freely share resources without incurring additional cost, and we develop a framework to understand this shared-resource behavior. We also demonstrate that this phenomenon is a characteristic of a specific class of networks that can be described using a well-defined function. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which these networks can correct errors using a different type of tensor, and we shed light on the underlying dynamics of the networks through the use of quantum channel matrix analysis. Our work paves the way for the development of network theories that seamlessly integrate efficient variational models, error correction, and phase transitions, and we provide examples of such networks in the form of supersymmetric SYK models and their chemical potential extensions.

Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks have demonstrated significant success in process-mining applications, surpassing traditional approaches in various predictive tasks. Building upon existing research, this study explores the effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks and Multi-layer Perceptron models with dropout in forecasting the type and timing of subsequent process activities. Unlike previous studies, we assess the performance of these models at distinct stages of a process, determined by event frequency and case duration. Our experiments reveal that the straightforward Multi-layer Perceptron often outperforms more complex deep-learning models in both prediction tasks. Consequently, we emphasize the need for caution when applying automated process-prediction techniques at different stages of a process, and we recommend using strong baselines such as simple Multi-layer Perceptrons to validate research results.

This paper presents a novel approach for clustering dynamic systems based solely on time-series data, which inherently accounts for the system's evolution over time. Current training methods often struggle with unreliable gradient calculations or inaccurate sentence representations. To address this, we've developed a mathematical model that considers various factors including how long microorganisms can survive, the speed of stars, and the dispersal of ejected material to evaluate the likelihood of detecting life that originated elsewhere. Our research suggests that by looking at exoplanets close to stable star clusters, we might be able to determine if life can be transferred from one system to another. We found that if microorganisms can survive for at least 10 million years, the chance of detecting life that originated elsewhere will be at least 50% for a significant portion of planetary systems with multiple stars. For example, for planetary systems with a large distance between stars of 100 AU or more, the chance of detecting life that originated elsewhere will be at least 37%. Our research also provides a method to estimate the timescales of potentially habitable exoplanets in a cluster, which can be used to further evaluate the possibility of life being transferred from one planetary system to another.

This approach involves using two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian. By gradually transitioning from the driver Hamiltonian to the problem Hamiltonian, it is possible to achieve the target ground state that represents the solution. Research suggests that incorporating non-stoquastic terms into the driver Hamiltonian may enhance the efficiency of quantum annealing, but it is also hindered by decoherence. We present case studies demonstrating that non-stoquastic Hamiltonians can lead to the complete failure of quantum annealing, whereas a specific decoherence process can prevent such failure. Specifically, when anti-ferromagnetic interactions are included in the Hamiltonian, we find that it is impossible to prepare the target ground state even with an infinite annealing time due to symmetry-induced block-diagonalization and crossing during the quantum annealing process. However, we also show that adding a particular type of decoherence enables the attainment of the ground state after quantum annealing, as the environment can break the symmetry present in isolated quantum systems. These counterintuitive findings provide valuable insights into the fundamental mechanisms underlying quantum annealing.

This mass window is defined as the difference between the masses of two distinct charged leptons, and its upper limit is the sum of their masses. A comprehensive dataset was collected from 70 online learning modules in both the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters, with the first 41 modules assigned before campus closure in Spring 2020. Three key metrics measured students' ability to stay on track: timely submission, early submission for extra credit, and engagement with modules. advanced versions of Liouville conformal field theory, characterized by increased symmetry. Toda conformal field theories can explicitly demonstrate this higher-spin symmetry, thanks to a path integral formulation rooted in Lie algebra. This document aims to illustrate how this enhanced symmetry is expressed within a rigorous probabilistic framework initially proposed by R. Rhodes, V. Vargas, and the first author. One of its notable aspects is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived from a rigorous derivation of the Miura transformation. Specifically, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, encapsulating higher-spin symmetry, are valid in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory; we also provide explicit expressions for the descendent fields, which were previously unidentified in the physics literature. This representation of descendent fields enables a systematic method for identifying degenerate fields in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories, leading to the conclusion that certain four-point correlation functions satisfy a third-order hypergeometric differential equation.

We introduce an axiomatic system, BZFC, by translating the ZFC axioms into a four-valued framework in a meticulous manner. Early studies employed non-invasive EEG-based BCIs to help paraplegics walk, but the limited resolution of these signals hindered their ability to perform more complex tasks. Using static models in such situations can lead to suboptimal performance, but modeling the underlying network dynamics can be challenging. Various creatures employ legs, wings, fins, and other mechanisms to navigate their surroundings. This report focuses on the movement of biological species, referred to as biolocomotion, and presents a computational method to identify biolocomotion in raw video footage. A distinctive characteristic of biolocomotion is the combination of an overall forward movement and an uneven oscillatory pattern, which tends to be absent in non-biological objects in motion. By leveraging this trait, along with differences between an object's overall movement and the localized movement of its parts, a developed algorithm can detect biolocomotion in tracked objects. An alternative algorithm, based on general features combined with machine learning, is also presented for comparison purposes. A comprehensive dataset of moving biological and non-biological objects in natural settings is provided, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing camouflage animals dataset. The results show that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the alternative approach, supporting the hypothesis that biolocomotion can be reliably detected based on its unique characteristics.

computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods, particularly those accelerated by Graphical Processing Units (GPUs). Some existing techniques include Neumann Series, Newton iteration, Chebyshev Iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In this work, we introduce a novel iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann', which builds upon the Neumann Series and offers a generalized approach by incorporating a computationally free update of the preconditioning matrix based on a specified 'inception depth'. The Nested Neumann algorithm has been proven to converge under certain conditions, achieve a convergence rate equivalent to its inception depth plus one, and exhibit optimal performance at inception depths of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for the Nested Neumann algorithm, which can be applied to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost. Notably, the Nested Neumann method can handle positive semi-definite matrices without additional modifications. We also demonstrate the applicability of the Nested Neumann algorithm to various analytical and numerical problems, including linear system inversion, matrix inverse computation, and differential equation solutions.

However, this adoption has inadvertently provided cybercriminals with opportunities to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain systems, targeting users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Most existing techniques for detecting malicious actors focus on individual wallet address behavior but fail to examine money trails. We introduce a heuristic-based approach that incorporates new features related to money trails to identify suspicious activities in cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we concentrate on cyclic behavior and uncover hidden patterns within temporal transaction graphs in a blockchain. We test our methods on Ethereum transaction data and discover that malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering exhibit distinct cyclic patterns. working has been on the rise, prompting Agile methodologies such as Scrum to be adapted to accommodate distributed teams. However, the COVID-19 pandemic brought about a new reality of full-time remote work, necessitating a deeper understanding of its effects on Scrum practitioners. This research employs a two-phased Multi-Method study to investigate the impact of working from home on Scrum practitioners. Phase one involves a qualitative survey to gauge the effects of remote work, while phase two proposes and validates a theoretical model using PLS-SEM with a sample of 200 software engineers who worked from home on Scrum projects. Our findings indicate that the model's latent variables are reliable and the hypotheses are statistically significant. Furthermore, an IPMA analysis highlights the benefits of remote work and Scrum adoption for project success. Notably, supporting the innate psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness in remote work environments is crucial. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that both remote work environments and Scrum practices contribute to project success, with Scrum acting as a key mediator in this process.

ulating particle collisions in complex fluid environments. Due to the disparity in time scales between fluid flow and particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive when dealing with large numbers of particles. A common workaround involves artificially lengthening the collision time, but this can skew simulation results. Our proposed method, the multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA), employs separate time steps for fluid flow, particle interactions, and collisions. is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains.

the use of negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite its importance, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a novel English reading comprehension dataset that demands reasoning about the implications of negated statements within paragraphs. Our dataset comprises paragraphs featuring diverse negation cues, along with corresponding question-answer pairs that require workers to assess the implications of negated statements. Additionally, we have workers create three types of passage edits, including paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing negation, resulting in clusters of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to answer without resorting to spurious shortcuts. CONDAQA comprises 14,182 question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues, and proves challenging for state-of-the-art models. Notably, even the top-performing model on CONDAQA, UnifiedQA-v2-3b, achieves only 42% on our consistency metric, significantly lower than human performance, which stands at 81%. To facilitate the development of future NLP models that can effectively handle negated language, we release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations under various conditions, as well as a fewshot benchmark that can be accessed through a user-friendly interface.

contrasting behaviors in the evolution of a quantum system over time: Quantum annealing involves gradual changes in the Hamiltonian to explore equilibrium phases, whereas quenching involves sudden, non-equilibrium changes. By combining statistical tools, such as neural network training, with quench data, the annealing gap's full functional behavior can be replicated. This knowledge can be used to develop optimized quantum annealing protocols, yielding practical time-to-solution benefits. Our findings are based on simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians, representing difficult exact cover problem instances.

bands for infinite layered nickelates, consisting of bands derived from $d$ and $s$-like orbitals, we examine the degree to which it can be reduced to a single-band Hubbard model. We determine that screening of the more mobile $s$-like band plays a crucial role. Without screening, a strongly-correlated band yields an antiferromagnetic ground state. For weak screening, strong correlations cause electrons to be expelled from the $s$-band, resulting in an undoped nickelate that remains a Mott insulator with half-filled $d$ orbitals. This scenario differs significantly from high-$T_c$ cuprates, and $s$-wave pairing would be more plausible in the superconducting state. Conversely, with strong screening, both $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands are partly filled and weakly coupled, leading to a self-doped $d$ band and tendencies towards $d$-wave pairing. Notably, in the regime of strong screening, mapping to a one-band model results in intriguing spectral weight transfers when a second $s$ band is also partly filled. Consequently, both one-band physics and a Kondo-lattice-like regime arise from the same two-orbital model, contingent upon the strength of electronic correlations and the size of the $s$-band pocket.

During this time, people have turned to social media platforms, particularly microblogging sites like Twitter, to express their emotions and cope with the situation. In this research, we analyzed Twitter posts using hashtags to understand public sentiment towards lockdowns, which has been a contentious issue with some people supporting the restrictions and others opposing them. By examining over 1 million tweets posted during the lockdown, we expressed our findings using various machine learning techniques to detect sentiment. Our analysis revealed that the majority of users (57%) expressed negative sentiments towards lockdowns, while the remainder (43%) had a more supportive attitude. This is a significant discovery, and further research is needed to validate our findings. Nevertheless, our study demonstrates the power of social media analysis in understanding public opinions and emotions towards critical events.

interlayer tunneling models were the primary theoretical frameworks for understanding cuprate superconductors. These models proposed Josephson coupling between CuO planes. However, measurements of interlayer magnetic penetration depth revealed that actual values exceeded the expected predictions from the interlayer tunneling model. Following the discovery of planar stripes and incommensurate charge ordering, it became plausible to consider Josephson coupling between these mesoscopic domains. Our research indicates that intralayer coupling exceeds interlayer coupling and is comparable to the condensation energy, leading to superconductivity through long-range phase coherence. Furthermore, the ratio of interlayer to intralayer penetration depths squared is directly proportional to the resistivity ratio near the superconducting transition temperature, consistent with observed measurements.

As a compact star's density increases with a falling sound speed, it deviates from the hydrodynamic behavior of an ideal fluid, making it crucial to investigate this phenomenon using a relativistic mean-field framework that incorporates dense matter properties.  However, since the sound speed's increase with density varies significantly depending on the equation of state, it's difficult to generalize its effects on the properties of compact stars.  This work delves into the relationship between sound speed and density in various conditions of compact stars and neutron matter, using well-known three-stream interactions that produce different boundary conditions for the chemical potential of the sigma meson.  The proposed new parameterizations of the sigma meson's interaction with nuclear matter have been tested against recent empirical data on the neutron matter equation of state, with the resulting compressed stars' properties found to align with those observed in pulsar and X-ray observations.  Moreover, the new parameterizations exhibit a more typical behavior of the sound speed, which may be a requirement for the equation of state that needs to be satisfied in order to reconcile the density of a compact star with its associated spin frequency.

Analytical calculations and numerical simulations were conducted to determine the impact of a small variation in this parameter on parallax estimations in astrometry. The simulations also revealed that the shift is highly dependent on the satellite's ecliptic latitude, which is attributed to an asymmetry in the scanning law used by the Gaia satellite.

two-dimensional solitons, such as the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for Bose-Einstein condensates, exhibit Galilean invariance. This property allows for the creation of families of moving solitons from stationary ones. However, finding models that enable stable self-accelation of solitons is a complex issue. Self-acceleration is typically associated with negative mass, a phenomenon observed in some quantum systems, but not in Bose-Einstein condensates. This review explores two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models capable of predicting stable self-accelation of solitons. One model involves a binary BEC trapped in an optical-lattice potential, where a pair of interacting 1D solitons can be accelerated by choosing an appropriate balance between the two components' interaction and the potential's modulation. The other model is based on a system of Gross-Pitaevskii equations for two resonantly coupled atomic components via a microwave field, which enables stable self-accelation of a "dark-dark" soliton. This scenario is of interest for implementing robust self-accelation of solitons in atomic gases.

These cations are known to emit light at longer wavelengths than their neutral counterparts, making them valuable tools for probing local plasma environments and tracing neutral gas in comets. However, a comprehensive understanding of their near-UV to visible properties is hindered by the limited availability of molecular data, particularly for small oxygen-containing cations. The simplicity of these devices presents opportunities for developing low-cost, custom-built spectroscopic instruments, such as multi-object or integral field spectrographs, that could significantly contribute to scientific research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet detection.

a model that aligns with distributed data across a network poses significant challenges. Specifically, Federated Learning is hindered by the communication bottleneck between nodes and the server. A common approach to alleviate this issue is for nodes to perform multiple local updates before sharing the results, yet this method often results in delayed convergence and biased models due to data heterogeneity. This work focuses on developing random walk learning algorithms to address the communication and data disparities. By utilizing direct connections between nodes, which are typically less resource-intensive, the model is passed from one node to another after each update. The challenge lies in navigating the data heterogeneity and uncertainty surrounding the data distributions. To achieve this, we formulate a sleeping multi-armed bandit framework to design an efficient node sampling strategy that produces variance-reduced gradient estimates and approaches the optimal sampling strategy in a sub-linear manner. We introduce an adaptive random walk learning algorithm, backed by theoretical convergence guarantees, and our numerical results demonstrate its superiority over existing random walk algorithms.

I analyzed North Carolina court cases from 1994 to 2009 to assess the effectiveness of mandating mental health treatment as a condition of probation in reducing recidivism. Comparing those who were required to undergo treatment with those who were not, I discovered that assignment to treatment significantly lowered the likelihood of recidivism by 17 percent over a three-year period. Deferred Neural Rendering achieves a balance between computational efficiency and realistic image quality. Extending this approach to articulated objects using skinned meshes offers numerous possibilities, but it requires the neural shading step to account for mesh deformations and alignment inaccuracies. To address these limitations, we propose Articulated Neural Rendering, a novel framework that builds on Deferred Neural Rendering and is specifically designed for virtual human avatars. Our approach outperforms both Deferred Neural Rendering and specialized avatar creation methods in user studies and evaluation metrics, demonstrating better temporal stability, level of detail, and overall plausibility.

In this research, we use graph neural networks to develop a quantifiable metric that can be used to gauge local disorder in materials. This metric captures the variety of atomic configurations in a given area and represents it as a continuous spectrum ranging from solid to liquid phases. We apply this innovative approach to three distinct scenarios with varying levels of disorder: solid-liquid interfaces, polycrystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries. Using aluminum as a test case, we demonstrate how our method can track the spatial and temporal changes of interfaces and define the boundary between order and disorder mathematically. Furthermore, we show how to derive gradients from our disorder fields that can be used to predict and analyze materials performance and failure. Our framework offers a practical and universally applicable approach to understanding the relationship between complex atomic structures and materials behavior.

We conducted a series of high-resolution simulations using the Arepo code and compared them to hydrodynamic simulations from the same initial conditions. This is the first investigation of magnetic fields in major mergers within a cosmologically accurate framework. Unlike previous non-cosmological simulations, we found that magnetic fields have a substantial influence on the final product of a merger. Although magnetic fields do not significantly affect overall galaxy properties, they do have a notable impact on structural characteristics. Our simulations reveal that magnetic fields lead to the formation of extended discs and spiral structures in mergers, whereas hydrodynamic simulations result in more compact remnants with ring-like morphologies. A resolution study confirms that global properties converge across different resolutions and physics models, but morphological differences emerge at sufficient resolution levels. This is attributed to the more efficient excitation of small-scale magnetic field amplification in high-resolution simulations, allowing for a stronger influence on gas dynamics.

To achieve this, we developed a groundbreaking 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network that takes into account infection patterns. This paper treats distinct GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a meta-learning approach to adapt GEC models to new domains without relying on pseudo data. In a real-world scenario, authorities might round average death rates to infer changes in suicide rates after a national emergency, which could be misleading due to the low suicide rates globally. This paper investigates the impact of rounding a non-negative discrete random variable to the nearest integer when estimating its average. We examine how the probability generating function, expected value, and variance of a proxy variable, obtained by dividing a random variable by a constant, capture the effects of data coarsening. Our analysis reveals that rounding has a minimal effect under certain conditions, but can significantly influence statistical inference in other cases, as demonstrated through two applications. The two distinct gadolinium ions in the centered honeycomb lattice give rise to a unique arrangement of honeycomb and triangular sublattices. self-interested agents with specific value systems is explored, where the focus is on finding mechanisms that maintain fairness and stability in their allocations. In the absence of monetary transactions, mechanisms are viewed as algorithms that operate based on reported rather than actual agent values. This study investigates whether mechanisms exist that consistently produce fair allocations in stable states and, specifically, examines two relaxations of envy-freeness, namely, fairness up to one good (EF1) and fairness up to any good (EFX). The existence of such mechanisms is confirmed, and two known algorithms, Round-Robin and a cut-and-choose method, are studied in the context of strategic agents. The results show that Round-Robin induces EF1 allocations in stable states, while the cut-and-choose method produces not only EFX allocations but also maximin share fairness for two agents, a property not observed in the non-strategic setting. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that a similar outcome holds for any mechanism with stable states that yield EFX allocations for two agents.

Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain translation. This enables us to (i) train more precise target networks by generating multiple outputs based on the same source image, incorporating both accurate translation and data augmentation to handle appearance variations, (ii) assign robust pseudo-labels to the target data by averaging the predictions of a source network on multiple translated versions of a single target image, and (iii) train and combine diverse networks in the target domain by adjusting the degree of stochasticity in the translations. Our results show significant improvements over recent strong baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised domain adaptation on two challenging semantic segmentation benchmarks. The source code for our project is available at https://github.com/elchiou/Beyond-deterministic-translation-for-UDA.

To understand this phenomenon, we compare the galaxy's H-alpha and broad-band images with similar data from four other spirals. Unlike conventional detectors, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks from the Earth's crust, which have been buried underground for over a billion years, accumulating damage from dark matter-induced nuclear recoils. Modern microscopy techniques allow for precise analysis of these damage tracks, making paleo-detectors potentially capable of detecting dark matter at much lower energy thresholds than current experiments. Thanks to their long integration times, paleo-detectors could offer exposures of 100 kilotonnes over a year, allowing them to probe dark matter interactions that are orders of magnitude below existing limits. This study uses advanced background modeling and statistical analysis to forecast the sensitivity of paleo-detectors, demonstrating their robustness to various uncertainties and assumptions. Even with high levels of uranium contamination, paleo-detectors could still detect dark matter interactions below current limits, potentially reaching the neutrino floor for dark matter masses below 10 GeV.

Although abundant unlabeled surveillance footage is easily accessible, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this data to develop meaningful re-identification representations. Most unsupervised and domain adaptation methods currently rely on these public datasets with removed labels, often requiring fine-tuning with unlabeled testing data due to the datasets' small sizes. Identifying which training examples contribute to inaccurate or unfair model predictions is crucial. Over the past decade, researchers have been exploring ways to compute the Shapley value of each training example, particularly in relation to validation accuracy and model fairness. However, existing methods have been limited to single models and do not account for the entire end-to-end machine learning pipeline, including data transformations and feature extraction. To address this, we introduce DataScope, a system that efficiently computes Shapley values across the entire pipeline, enabling effective data debugging for machine learning training. DataScope achieves this through a novel algorithmic framework for a specific type of pipeline, referred to as a canonical pipeline, which combines a relational algebra query and a K-nearest-neighbor classifier. Our results show that DataScope is significantly faster than state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable or even improved effectiveness in data debugging.

By establishing a threshold for radio luminosity, we cataloged radio sources within the core and a specific radius around the clusters, using a statistical method to determine if the number of sources correlates with collision rates and masses. Our analysis found a clear link between the number of radio sources in the core and collision rates or masses, but no such connection in the surrounding region. Five of the sources are likely to be neutron stars or black holes, with their presence influenced by collision rates, while one is a potential black hole candidate and ten remain unidentified. Once we accounted for verified cluster members, the correlation between the number of sources and collision rates or masses became even more significant. This outcome is consistent with previous simulations predicting that collision rates would be a poor indicator of black hole activity in clusters. Further research will help us better understand the distribution of black holes in clusters, offering new insights into the dynamics of these celestial bodies.

To better understand this problem, we develop a theoretical framework to examine its implications and worst-case scenarios. This analysis leads us to propose a novel task: supervised hypergraph reconstruction, where we aim to recover a real-world hypergraph from its projected graph, utilizing domain-specific knowledge. 

To tackle the challenge of reconstructing hypergraph data, we start by examining the distribution of hyperedges in the projection, which enables us to create a two-module framework: (1) we design an efficient sampling strategy to significantly reduce the search space of potential hyperedges; (2) we develop a hyperedge classifier in two variants, which effectively captures structural features in the projection. Our approach is extensively validated through experiments, which demonstrate that it outperforms all baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on challenging datasets. Our code and data are available for download.

Specifically, when one agent learns from pre-collected data, it may adopt suboptimal behavior from less competent peers, undermining the team's overall performance. To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that promotes diversity in agent-wise trajectories. By decomposing global rewards into individual credits using an attention-based mechanism, our approach reconstructs datasets to prioritize high-quality experiences. This enables agents to share successful strategies and refine their policies using a graph attention network-based critic. Evaluations on various environments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, particularly in scenarios with significant disparities in data quality.
